title: Simplicial Embeddings Improve Sample Efficiency in Actor–Critic Agents
claim: Non-stationary targets degrade optimization, representation rank and neuron activity, but a simple structural embedding layer largely restores stability.
layout: 3 panels in one row, shared legend on top, line plots over training
description: A single horizontal strip of three line plots with a shared legend on top. The legend has three colors: light blue for Stationary, orange for Non-stationary, and green for Non-stationary + SEM. The left panel plots loss against training. The blue curve falls smoothly. The orange and green curves jump up in sawtooth spikes every time the targets are shuffled, then decay again. The green curve recovers to a lower loss than orange. The middle panel plots effective rank, where higher is better. Orange stays flat or declines and blue stays flat, while green climbs steadily to the highest value. The right panel plots the percentage of dormant neurons, where lower is better. Orange spikes sharply to 30–50% at each shuffle. Blue and green stay low, near 1–8%. The eye goes first to the orange spikes and the green curve that diverges from them.
caption: Training dynamics on CIFAR-10 with stationary vs. non-stationary targets. In the stationary regime (fixed targets), losses decrease smoothly, neuron dormancy and effective rank remains controlled, suggesting stable representation learning. In the non-stationary regime (targets shuffled every 20 epochs), the model exhibits higher variance in losses, increased dormant neuron rates, and reduced effective rank. The addition of SEM mitigates this instability. Experiments are averaged over 3 independent seeds, with shaded areas reporting 95% confidence intervals.
abstract: Recent works have proposed accelerating the wall-clock training time of actor-critic methods via the use of large-scale environment parallelization; unfortunately, these can sometimes still require large number of environment interactions to achieve a desired level of performance. Noting that well-structured representations can improve the generalization and sample efficiency of deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents, we propose the use of simplicial embeddings: lightweight representation layers that constrain embeddings to simplicial structures. This geometric inductive bias results in sparse and discrete features that stabilize critic bootstrapping and strengthen policy gradients. When applied to FastTD3, FastSAC, and PPO, simplicial embeddings consistently improve sample efficiency and final performance across a variety of continuous- and discrete-control environments, without any loss in runtime speed.
